label: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, pool-exhaustion, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, and stopped on diagnosed after 10 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. It was offered one write action (rollback_deploy), as in week 4; in an evaluation run its gate only plans an action the diagnosis names: nobody is asked, and nothing runs. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Code planned the action its diagnosis named (redeploy payments-api: PROVIDER_BREAKER on (unchanged), CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT cents (unchanged), REFUND_CONNECTION kept -> returned); in an evaluation run nobody is asked, and nothing ran. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing (klaxon.faults).

case.name: pool-exhaustion
case.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
case.right_answer: The fault's recorded cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500.
case.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

fault.name: pool-exhaustion
fault.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
fault.cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500
expected_symptoms: the pool runs dry about 40 to 50 s after the deploy; then POST /payments takes 5 to 8 s (a worker thread, then the pool's 5 s wait) and fails with a 500: the p95 latency passes 7 s, and the 5xx share passes 70% within a minute
the payments API logs 'unhandled error' with PoolTimeout: no connection within 5 s
its health check fails too, so docker marks it unhealthy, while PostgreSQL itself is up
the traffic's clients retry and give up: many payments end with their outcome unknown, and arrivals past 64 in flight are shed
the money check passes: a payment that never got a connection was never charged, and one charged before its answer was lost is confirmed by its webhook
fault.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

diagnosis.hypothesis: After the payments-api deploy at 08:39:07 (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept), the psycopg database connection pool is exhausted. POST /payments and POST /payments/{id}/refunds both wait for a connection until PoolTimeout and return 500. That gives the 66% 5xx rate and the 7 s p95 latency. The most likely culprit is REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, which would make refund requests keep their DB connection and starve the pool. This is an inference: I saw the settings change and the timing, but no trace or metric showing which requests hold the connections. Provider calls are fast, so a slow provider is not the cause. Not ruled out: another change in the same deploy, or another DB client holding connections. A few 503s on POST /payments began at 08:38:31, before the deploy, so they have a separate or earlier cause that I did not investigate.

evidence.shows: The symptom is real: 500s on POST /payments appear at 08:40:31 at about 2.9/s, and 201s fall from about 3.2/s to about 1/s. Small numbers of 503s appear from 08:38:31.

payments-api was recreated at 08:39:07 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, PROVIDER_BREAKER=on and CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents. The other services were created at 08:37:41, so payments-api is the only service changed shortly before the 500s.
The payments-api errors are psycopg PoolTimeout exceptions on POST /payments, many per second at 08:40:34-35.

A failing POST /payments trace lasts 6.6 s with error.type psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout. It has only Redis spans and no provider call, so the request waited for a DB connection and never reached the provider.
Calls to the provider are fast (p95 about 5 ms), so slow provider calls are not what holds the pool.
Refund requests on payments-api take 5.0-6.2 s each at 08:40:03-08:40:18, which fits waiting for pool connections.
A refund trace is a 5.0 s 500 with error.type PoolTimeout and no database or provider spans, so refunds also time out waiting for a connection. This does not show who holds the connections.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to the settings it ran before the 08:39:07 deploy. This stops new pool exhaustion if REFUND_CONNECTION=kept or another change in that deploy is the cause. Then check that the 5xx rate and POST /payments latency recover, and rerun money_check. A rollback repairs nothing already booked, so review the payments and refunds that failed or were left half done during the incident.

diagnosis.blast_radius: payments-api is recreated and pauses while it restarts, so requests in that window fail. Other services are untouched. The rollback also reverts PROVIDER_BREAKER and CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT to their earlier values, which I did not check. If the cause is not in that deploy, the rollback will not fix the errors.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: If the rollback makes things worse, redeploy payments-api with the settings from the 08:39:07 deploy (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept) and look for the cause elsewhere, for example DB connections held by other clients.
